content: Neotyphodium is a genus of endophytic fungi that are asexual and seed-borne. These fungi form symbiotic relationships with cool-season grasses and grow intercellularly within the aerial tissues of their host plants. They can be found in various parts of the plant, including the shoot apical meristems, leaf sheaths, leaf blades, inflorescences, seeds, and embryos. Taxonomic Considerations Neotyphodium species are closely related to the teleomorphic (sexual) species of the genus Epichloë. Many Neotyphodium species have evolved through interspecific hybridization involving Epichloë species. Molecular phylogenetic studies have shown that asexual Neotyphodium species are derived either from individual Epichloë species or, more commonly, from hybrids involving at least two ancestral Epichloë species. As a result, the genus Neotyphodium is taxonomically and evolutionarily linked to Epichloë. According to botanical nomenclature, Neotyphodium refers to the asexual or vegetative state of the fungus, while Epichloë refers to the sexual state. Life Cycle The life cycle of Neotyphodium is unique because it propagates vegetatively through vertical transmission. This means the fungal mycelium grows into newly developing host tillers, which are individual grass plants. Neotyphodium and some Epichloë species infect new grass plants by growing into the seeds of their host grasses and subsequently infecting the seedlings. In contrast, the sexual state, which occurs only in Epichloë fungi, leads to a condition known as choke disease. In this disease, the fungal outgrowth forms a stroma that engulfs the grass inflorescences, suppressing seed production. The stroma eventually releases meiospores (ascospores), which enable horizontal transmission of the fungus to new plants. Effects on Grass Plants and Herbivores Vertically transmitted symbionts like Neotyphodium are hypothesized to evolve mutualistic relationships with their hosts because their reproductive success is closely tied to the fitness of the host plant. Neotyphodium species can confer several benefits to their host grasses, including enhanced growth, improved drought tolerance, and increased resistance to herbivores and pathogens. The resistance to herbivores is largely attributed to alkaloids produced by the endophytes. However, the relationship between grass and endophyte is not always mutualistic. Under nutrient-poor soil conditions, the interaction can become antagonistic. Neotyphodium Alkaloids Neotyphodium species produce several classes of alkaloids, which play a critical role in deterring herbivores and protecting the host plant. These include: 1. Ergoline Alkaloids: These are ergot alkaloids, structurally derived from 4-prenyl tryptophan. Ergovaline is one of the most abundant ergot alkaloids in endophyte-symbiotic grasses. It consists of an ergoline moiety attached to a bicyclic tripeptide containing L-proline, L-alanine, and L-valine. 2. Indole-Diterpenoids: An example is lolitrem B, which has biological activity against mammalian herbivores and some insects. 3. Peramine: This pyrrolopyrazine alkaloid is thought to be synthesized from L-arginine and pyrrolidine-5-carboxylate, a precursor of L-proline. Peramine acts as an insect-feeding deterrent. 4. Loline Alkaloids: These are 1-aminopyrrolizidines with an oxygen atom linking the bridgehead carbons 2 and 7. They are biosynthesized from L-proline and L-homoserine. Lolines exhibit insecticidal and insect-deterrent properties comparable to nicotine. Not all Neotyphodium species produce all these alkaloids, but many produce up to three classes of them. Species of Neotyphodium The genus Neotyphodium includes the following species: Neotyphodium aotearoae Neotyphodium australiense Neotyphodium chilense Neotyphodium chisosum Neotyphodium coenophialum Neotyphodium gansuense Neotyphodium huerfanum Neotyphodium lolii Neotyphodium melicicola Neotyphodium occultans Neotyphodium siegelii Neotyphodium starrii Neotyphodium tembladerae Neotyphodium typhinum Neotyphodium uncinatum
